reconcile.connective: Gill reads the accounts as sequential stages: an initial acquaintance through John the Baptist, then a later, formal call to full-time discipleship.

discrepancy.connective: D. F. Strauss judged the two calling scenes irreconcilable, dismissing the harmonizing sequence as "violence to the gospels out of harmonistic zeal."

skeptic.name: D. F. Strauss
skeptic.work: The Life of Jesus Critically Examined
skeptic.attribution: D. F. Strauss (1808-1874), The Life of Jesus Critically Examined (1846)

excerpts.excerpt_text: These two brethren had been the disciples of John, as Theophylact thinks, and which seems agreeable to Joh 1:35 and though through John's pointing out Christ unto them, they had some knowledge of him, and conversation with him, yet they abode with him but for that day, Joh 1:37 and afterwards returned to their master; and upon his imprisonment, betook themselves to their former employment: from whence Christ now calls them to be his disciples, saying "follow me" …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill frames the John 1 meeting as a prior, informal acquaintance and Matthew's 'follow me' as the later, formal call, directly reconciling why Matthew's calling scene reads as a first encounter despite John having them meet earlier.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible, on Luke 5:1-11 (1706-1714)
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats Luke's miraculous-draught scene as the same event Matthew and Mark summarize more briefly, and traces Peter and Andrew's attachment to Jesus through stages beginning at John's baptism -- the fullest harmonizing treatment of all three narrative tensions in this contradiction.
